title: Which favors will you deny?
hookLine: the refrain repeated thirty-one times: which of your Lord's favors will you deny (55:13)

cards: The Prophet ﷺ once recited a whole surah to his companions, a report in Tirmidhi says, and they listened to the end in silence. Then he told them another audience had answered it better.

Not with silence: with words, every time a certain line came round. And it came round a lot. In Surah Ar-Rahman, one question returns again and again, after fruit, after the seas, after the rising places of the sun.
Today, that question, and who answered it.

teach.b: Verse thirteen, the first of thirty-one times it appears. Pickthall: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?" In Arabic: fa-bi-ayyi ala'i rabbikuma tukadhdhiban.
Two things hide in the grammar. First, rabbikuma, your Lord, and tukadhdhiban, you deny, are dual: they speak to two.

teach.h: SPOKEN TO TWO: JINN AND HUMANS.
teach.b: Verse thirty-three addresses the company of jinn and humans, and commentators read the whole refrain as spoken to both. Second, ala'. Pickthall says favors, the usual reading: blessings, bounties, gifts.
Some commentators add that ala' can also carry the sense of wonders, signs of power. So the line asks which of these gifts, and which of these marvels, will you call a lie?
Notice it's a question, not an accusation. The surah lists a gift, then stops and asks. Fruit and palm trees: which will you deny?
The two seas and their pearls: which will you deny? Even warnings get the refrain, as if being warned were a kindness too. Now the report.
The better audience, the Prophet told his companions, was the jinn. Each time he reached the refrain, they replied that they denied none of their Lord's favors, and praise belonged to Him.
Some listeners still answer the refrain that way under their breath. On this reading, the repetition isn't filler. It's a stop after every blessing, long enough to notice it.

how: Surah Ar-Rahman is often recited aloud, and some Muslims, hearing the refrain, quietly answer that they deny none of their Lord's favors, following the report in Tirmidhi.

o: favors and blessings, and for some, wonders
hidden beings made of smokeless fire
the warnings sent to people who deny

games.q: the refrain of Ar-Rahman — tap the pairs.

s: the refrain appears in Ar-Rahman thirty-one times
it returns again and again, after gifts and after warnings.
the refrain is spoken to humans alone
its verbs are dual, and commentators read it as addressed to jinn and humans.
the refrain only follows descriptions of gifts
it follows warnings too, as if a warning were also a kindness.

games.q: the Prophet recites Ar-Rahman to his companions, and they listen in silence. what does he tell them, in the report in Tirmidhi?
o: that silence is the best answer.
that the jinn answered it better.
games.why: he said the jinn answered better: at each refrain they replied that they denied none of their Lord's favors.

practice: Let one ordinary gift come to mind, the breath you're taking, the light in the room, someone who texted you this week, and ask quietly: which of His favors?
If you pray, answer as the report says the jinn did, that you deny none of them; if not, simply name the gift and move to the next.

wordCard.voice: Ala': the favors, and wonders, of the Lord that Surah Ar-Rahman's refrain asks thirty-one times whether you will deny. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: so which of the favors of your Lord will you two deny? The dual endings speak to two.

carryVoice: Your line: which of his favors? The refrain is a pause after every gift. Day six hundred five, done.
